title: The emperor’s notebook
told: from the notebook of Marcus Aurelius

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? is there something you keep saving for next month? a call, a trip, a sorry.
options: then this one is for you. an emperor had the same habit.
hold it in mind. you’ll know what to do with it by the end.
good. keep this one anyway. it’s warmer than it sounds.

steps.line: About eighteen centuries ago, Marcus Aurelius ruled Rome. He spent many of his last years in cold army camps on the far frontier, by the Danube river.
At night, by lamplight, he wrote notes to himself, in Greek. Not speeches. Reminders. Their old title is simply “To Himself.”

steps.q: The most powerful man in the world keeps coming back to one subject in his notes. What is it?
steps.why: His own death. Not to frighten himself. You’ll see where it lands.

steps.line: He reminded himself that he would die, like everyone. Alexander the Great and his mule driver, he wrote, ended up in the same place.

steps.q: Why would an emperor remind himself that a great king and a mule driver end up the same?
o: To comfort himself his enemies would die too
Power and fame don’t outlast anyone
steps.why: Death evens everyone out. For a man with every kind of power, that kept his eyes on what he could still do well.

steps.line: He wrote: “Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good.”
steps.label: an old translation

steps.q: A tutor lent Marcus the lecture notes of one teacher, and Marcus thanks him for it. Whose notes?
o: Epictetus’s, a man born a slave
steps.why: Meditations 1.7: he thanks his tutor Rusticus for lending him Epictetus’s lectures, and quotes Epictetus later on. The most powerful man alive, learning from a former slave.

steps.line: His notes survived him, copied by hand for centuries. Today we call them the Meditations, and people still read them.
steps.label: later

steps.line: Today, a skull, an hourglass, two Latin words: memento mori, “remember that you will die.” It’s the same idea, and it’s really about today.
steps.label: today

steps.q: An old Roman story: in a victory parade, someone rode behind the general whispering a warning. What?
steps.why: Tertullian, around 200 AD, tells it: “Look behind you; remember you are a man.” Later artists turned the idea into memento mori skulls.

say: here’s what i love. marcus was a stoic, and stoics taught that death is natural, nothing to fear, and worth remembering.
not because life is grim. because a life you remember is short gets clearer. the good thing you keep postponing comes closer.

steps.q: Someone gets “memento mori” tattooed and says it means “nothing matters, so who cares.” From Marcus’s note, what would he say?
o: Time is short, so today matters more
Forget death and just enjoy today
steps.why: For Marcus, remembering death pointed straight back at today: while it is in your power, be good.

today.say: pick the one thing you keep saving for next month: the call, the thank-you, the sorry. do the first small step of it today.
options: while it is in your power. that’s exactly it.
that counts. you’ve brought it closer already.

sources: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 4.17, trans. George Long (1862): “Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good.”
Meditations 6.24: Alexander the Macedonian and his mule driver were brought to the same state by death.
Book 1 closes “among the Quadi, on the Gran”; Book 2 is headed “at Carnuntum”: written during the Marcomannic Wars on the Danube frontier (c. 170s CE).
Written in Greek; the Greek title is usually given as “To Himself” (Ta eis heauton).
